summary:
Región de Los Lagos stands under Chile's national framework: Gender Identity Law 21,120, in force since 27 December 2019, applies in the region on the same terms as elsewhere in the country. Adults may change their registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry without therapy or surgery. People aged 14 to 18 must apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents, and those under 14 cannot use the law, though the statute recognises them as transgender. On 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, and that ruling applies only to that case.

Discrimination and hate-motivated offending are governed nationally. The 2012 Zamudio Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates offer a third sex option for intersex children, a provision in place since 2006.

Transphobic violence remains documented at national level. A young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as Chile's largest hate crime; the perpetrator, an acquaintance, confessed. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour at a Santiago hotel, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Detention carries specific rules across the prison system. Gendarmería de Chile's national director signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, providing placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation, including access rules for trans visitors.

Care access follows national policy. The public health system has funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013, and a 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centres to register transgender patients by their social name. Circular 7 of June 2024 suggested deferring the initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published; the Medical College noted that physicians may still prescribe. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court, by seven votes to three, annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law, which had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents.

Entry and removal rules reference gender identity. The Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that recognised asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.

Restrictive proposals are active but non-binding. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report, 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions, a non-binding recommendation to eliminate the Gender Identity Support Program, restrict minors' progressive autonomy, ban hormonal treatment for minors and repeal the circular protecting gender identity in schools.

Within that national picture, Región de Los Lagos is one data point among sixteen regions rather than a separate legal regime. Movilh's XXIV annual report (HECHOS 2025) records a national total of 3,620 cases and complaints of discrimination in 2025, up 27.1% and the highest figure in 24 years; only Valparaíso (-17.56%) and Metropolitana (-14.35%) recorded a fall, while the other 14 regions rose. Los Lagos accounted for 3.14% of nationally documented abuse cases, the fourth-largest regional share, with a +9.09% year-on-year rise in 2025.
tangentialFactors:
Outright International's Chile country dossier, published March 12, 2026, carries no division-specific information and no Los Lagos-specific legal, incident or enforcement finding, so the national score is the basis for this division: same-sex marriage and adoption legal since March 2022; the hate-crime law has covered sexual orientation and gender identity since 2012; legal gender recognition by self-determination since 2019; a third sex option on birth certificates since 2006.

Movilh reads the 2025 regional distribution as hatred expanding into regions with less public debate, which underpins the mid-range reading of the Los Lagos share and suggests the regional figure reflects reporting conditions as much as incidence.

The direction of national travel is contested inside the legislature. In the 2025-26 rollback, the Chilean congress excluded the Gender Identity Support Program (PAIG) from the 2026 budget bill, an action condemned by civil society groups and the national ombuds for children, while the non-binding CEI 57 report of 15 May 2025 presses further restrictions that carry no legal force.

The regional pattern is uniform rather than urban-concentrated: fourteen of sixteen regions rose in 2025, and the two that fell are the largest metropolitan areas, which is the opposite of a capital-centred distribution.
localsOnly:
In November 2025 Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program through the 2026 Budget Law, but the Ministry of Health-run programme continues to provide support in medical centres; the Crece con Orgullo programme has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17.

The 2011 Ministry of Health circular requiring all care centres to register transgender patients by their social name remains the operative registration rule for residents using health services, and publicly funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy have been available since 2013.

Residents aged 14 to 18 seeking legal gender recognition must petition a family court with psychosocial and family-context antecedents; adults proceed administratively through the Civil Registry. The Constitutional Court's 9 April 2025 ruling on the age wording applies only to the case before it and does not by itself open the procedure to under-14s.

Defendants and detainees in the region are covered by the Gendarmería de Chile protocol, which governs placement by assumed gender, segmented housing, entry examinations and access for trans visitors, monitored by a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives.

Movilh's XXIV annual report (HECHOS 2025) does not reproduce the 2024 share for Los Lagos, so the +9.09% year-on-year figure for 2025 cannot be checked against a stated prior-year base within this edition.

No Los Lagos-specific violence incident, detention case, document refusal or health-service denial is sourced here; the 2023 murder and the September 2021 Santiago hotel attack are national findings and neither is recorded as occurring in this region.
